newsitem.title: JAPAN: INSTANT VIEW - Japan July customs-cleared trade.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Japan July customs-cleared trade.

text.p: Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus jumped 69.7 percent in July from a year earlier to 849.08 billion yen, the Ministry of Finance said on Monday.
The surplus with the United States grew 35.7 percent to 420.55 billion yen.
MINEKO SASAKI-SMITH, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CS FIRST BOSTON:

"This trend is very much disturbing. It marks the fourth consecutive month of surge so...as we go into the IMF-World Bank meetings, inevitably Japan's trade surplus will be on the mind of U.S. decision-makers. They don't want to politicise it in a sense because they exploited the success of the results-oriented negotiations so they are playing it low, but in reality it is very much on their minds."
RON BEVACQUA, ECONOMIST, MERRILL LYNCH JAPAN:

"The trade surplus is rising, but the market is focussed on monetary factors. We still see the yen depreciating because of interest differentials, capital flows and faster, narrow money growth in Japan."
JANE BERRYMAN, FIXED INCOME ANALYST, TECHNICAL DATA

"Although the overall trend continues to favour a widening of Japan's surplus, clearly this number is below consensus. But I think the thing that is pertinent right now is that the surplus with the U.S. at 420.5 billion (yen). Arriving today is U.S. deputy trade representative (Jeffrey Lang)...this unfortunately is going to be more fodder (for him) to really make hay with in regards to putting pressure on the Japanese.

Although the pressure on the currency now seems fairly contained...keep your eyes peeled...on U.S. officials, who might make some bearish commentary on trade and the dollar might experience pressure later on in the day as a result.

"I think now we are in a different environment whereby the Asian currency crisis would have an impact on the overall Japanese trade balance come six months ahead. So I think the U.S. will be temperate in its comments relating to any rise in the surplus at this juncture. So we think the dollar/yen, obviously, is moving higher and the market is beginning to account for the Asian equation more so than just the bilateral surplus with the U.S.

"Also European currencies have been weakening against the dollar for some time now and that should have an impact on the overall surplus some time from now. It was a well-expected figure and should be dollar supportive in the interim."
